{{Short description|Unit of risk – one-in-a-million chance of death}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2020}}

A '''micromort''' (from [[micro-]] and [[Wikt:mortality|mortality]]) is a unit of [[risk]] defined as a one-in-a-million chance of [[death]]. Micromorts are usually assigned per event, or per unit of time a person is exposed to something.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fry |first1=A.M. |last2=Harrison |first2=A. |last3=Daigneault |first3=M. |title=Micromorts - what is the risk? |journal=British Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery |date=February 2016 |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=230–231 |doi=10.1016/j.bjoms.2015.11.023 |pmid=26747014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Walker |first1=KF |last2=Cohen |first2=AL |last3=Walker |first3=SS |last4=Allen |first4=KM |last5=Baines |first5=DL |last6=Thornton |first6=Jg |title=The dangers of the day of birth |journal=BJOG |date=May 2014 |volume=121 |issue=6 |pages=714–718 |doi=10.1111/1471-0528.12544 |pmid=24521517 |s2cid=24808758 }}</ref> Micromorts can be used to measure the riskiness of various day-to-day activities. A '''microprobability''' is a one-in-a million chance of some event; thus, a micromort is the microprobability of mortality from an event, or the health impacts of an event. The micromort concept was introduced by [[Ronald A. Howard]] who pioneered the modern practice of [[decision analysis]].<ref>{{cite conference
 |last=Howard |first=R. A. |author-link=Ronald A. Howard
 |title=On making life and death decisions
 |editor= J. Richard |editor2=C. Schwing |editor3=Walter A. Albers
 |conference=Societal Risk Assessment: How Safe Is Safe Enough? General Motors Research Laboratories
 |publisher=Plenum Press |location=New York
 |isbn=0306405547 |year=1980
}}</ref>

Micromorts for future activities can only be rough assessments, as specific circumstances will always have an impact. However, past historical rates of events can be used to provide a rough estimate.

A related and somewhat opposing unit is the [[microlife]], which measures statistical improvements to life expectancy from an activity—one example being regular [[aerobic exercise]].

* Travelling 8.8 miles (14&nbsp;km) by [[motorcycle]] (collision, UK)<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Reported road casualties Great Britain, annual report: 2024 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/reported-road-casualties-great-britain-annual-report-2024/reported-road-casualties-great-britain-annual-report-2024 |access-date=2026-04-23 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Road traffic estimates in Great Britain, 2024: Headline figures |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/road-traffic-estimates-in-great-britain-2024/road-traffic-estimates-in-great-britain-2024-headline-figures |access-date=2026-04-23 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>

* Travelling 370 miles (600&nbsp;km) by [[car]] (collision, UK)<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />
* Travelling 1,000 miles (1,600&nbsp;km) by [[Jet aircraft|jet airplane]] (collision)<ref name="howard" />
* Travelling 6,000 miles (10,000&nbsp;km) by [[train]] (collision)<ref>{{cite report|date=March 2023 |title=Safety Overview 2023 |url=https://www.era.europa.eu/system/files/2023-03/Safety%20Overview%202023.pdf |publisher=European Union Agency For Railways |at=p. 7, fig. 6 }}</ref>

== Value of a micromort ==
=== Willingness to pay ===
An application of micromorts is measuring the value that humans place on risk. For example, a person can consider the amount of money they would be [[willingness to pay|willing to pay]] to avoid a one-in-a-million chance of death (or conversely, the amount of money [[willingness to accept|they would receive to accept]] a one-in-a-million chance of death). When offered this situation, people claim a high number. However, when looking at their day-to-day actions (e.g., how much they are willing to pay for safety features on cars), a typical value for a micromort is around $50 (in 2009).<ref>{{cite journal
| last=Howard |first=R. A. |author-link=Ronald A. Howard
| title=Microrisks for Medical Decision Analysis
| journal=International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
| volume=5
| year=1989
| pages=357–370
| pmid=10295520
| doi=10.1017/S026646230000742X
| issue=3
|s2cid=37558060 }}</ref><ref name="russell">{{cite book
| last1=Russell |first1=Stuart
|last2=Norvig |first2=Peter
| title=Artificial Intelligence
|edition=3rd
|isbn=978-0-13-604259-4
|publisher=Prentice Hall
| year=2009
|page=616
}}</ref> This is not to say the $50 valuation should be taken to mean that a human life (1 million micromorts) is valued at $50,000,000. Rather, people are [[Marginal utility|less inclined to spend money after a certain point]] to increase their safety. This means that analyzing risk using the micromort is more useful when using small risks, not necessarily large ones.<ref name="russell"/>

=== Value of a statistical life ===
Government agencies use a nominal [[Value of a Statistical Life]] (VSL) – or [[Value for Preventing a Fatality]] (VPF) – to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of expenditure on safeguards.  For example, in the UK, the VSL is £1&nbsp;million&nbsp;[[GBP]] in 1997 value (equivalent to £{{Inflation|GBP|1|1997|r=0}}&nbsp;million in {{Inflation/year|UK}}{{Inflation/fn|UK}}).<ref>{{cite book|publisher=[[Department for Transport]] |title=Transport analysis guidance |chapter= Unit A4.1: Social Impact Appraisal |date=January 2014 |location=London |author=[[Government of the United Kingdom]] |url=https://www.gov.uk/guidance/transport-analysis-guidance-tag|chapter-url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/63a32a8d8fa8f539198d9bf3/TAG_Unit_A4.1_-_Social-impact-appraisal_Nov_2022_Accessible_v1.0.pdf.pdf |page=6 }}</ref> Since road improvements have the effect of lowering the risk of large numbers of people by a small amount, the [[UK Department for Transport]] essentially prices a reduction of 1 micromort at £1.60. The [[United States Department of Transportation|US Department of Transportation]] uses a VSL of US$6.2 million, pricing a micromort at US$6.20.<ref>US Department of Transportation, "Treatment of the Economic Value of a Statistical Life in Departmental Analyses—2011 Interim Adjustment", 2011, http://www.dot.gov/policy/transportation-policy/treatment-economic-value-statistical-life [https://www.transportation.gov/policy/transportation-policy/treatment-economic-value-statistical-life]</ref>

==Chronic risks==
Micromorts are best used to measure the size of ''acute'' risks, i.e. immediate deaths. Risks from lifestyle, exposure to [[air pollution]], and so on are ''chronic'' risks, in that they do not kill straight away, but reduce life expectancy. Ron Howard included such risks in his original 1979 work,<ref name="howard" /> for example, an additional one micromort from:
* Drinking 0.5 liter of [[wine]] (cirrhosis of the liver)<ref name="howard">* Howard, Ron {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120714164305/http://stanford-online.stanford.edu/sdrmda61w/session10b/slides/sld031.htm|title=Risky Decisions}} (Slide show), Stanford University</ref>
* [[Smoking]] 1.4 cigarettes (cancer, heart disease)<ref name="howard"/> 
* Spending 1 hour in a coal mine (black lung disease)<ref name="howard" />
* Spending 3 hours in a coal mine (accident)<ref name="howard" />
* Living 2 days in New York or Boston in 1979 (air pollution)<ref name="howard" />
* Living 2 months with a smoker (cancer, heart disease)<ref name="howard" />
* Drinking Miami water for 1 year (cancer from chloroform)<ref name="howard" />
* Eating 100 charcoal-broiled steaks (cancer from benzopyrene)<ref name="howard" />
* Traveling 6000 miles (10,000&nbsp;km) by jet (cancer due to increased background radiation)<ref name="esr">{{cite web|url=http://www.myesr.org/html/img/pool/15_Loose_Reinhard_Radiation_Dose_Issues_and_Risk.pdf|title=Radiation dose issues and risk|publisher=European Society of Radiology|access-date=2013-11-18|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219020315/http://www.myesr.org/html/img/pool/15_Loose_Reinhard_Radiation_Dose_Issues_and_Risk.pdf|archive-date=19 February 2014}}</ref>

Chronic risks are typically measured in terms of individual life expectancy, rather than death rates. Therefore, chronic risks are better measured with a related unit, the [[microlife]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2026|reason=https://www.epa.gov/environmental-economics/mortality-risk-valuation#difference seems to contradict}}
